findings.issue: The new regression test Issue_WhenAnotherContextCommitsALaterDateWhileThisOneRaces_TheRetryRefuses_InsteadOfRegressingLastDate asserts only InvalidOperationException plus the message "date is earlier than the last issued number" — a string that is byte-identical to the pre-loop MaxAsync refusal at OfficialNumberService.cs:190. The test therefore cannot, by itself, distinguish the guard it exists to protect (the in-loop recheck at line 230, reached only after a lost race and a ReloadAsync) from the pre-existing pre-loop guard. I confirmed externally that it really is the in-loop guard that fires (see notes: a standalone Microsoft.Data.Sqlite probe shows the MAX statement is stepped inside ExecuteReader, so the interceptor's later ExecuteUpdate cannot change the value MaxAsync returns; attempt 1 therefore sees the stale tracked LastDate, loses the concurrency check, reloads, and attempt 2 refuses), so the test is non-vacuous today. But that guarantee rests on an EF/SQLite execution-ordering detail the test never asserts: if it ever shifted, the test would pass on the pre-loop check and silently stop guarding the retry path.
findings.fix: After `Assert.Contains("date is earlier than the last issued number", ex.Message, StringComparison.Ordinal);` add two assertions on the pinned tracked instance, which only the catch block's ReloadAsync can refresh: `Assert.Equal(2, stale.LastSeq);` and `Assert.Equal(laterDate, stale.LastDate);`. Both are false if the pre-loop check refused (the row would still read LastSeq 1 / seedDate), so they pin the refusal to the post-reload path the finding is about.

findings.issue: The refusal message "official numbering refused: date is earlier than the last issued number" is now duplicated as a literal at line 190 (pre-loop) and line 232 (in-loop). Two copies of the same contract string can drift, and any future caller that maps this refusal by message (there is no caller yet — B3's correspondence approval will be the first) would then map only one of the two paths.
findings.fix: Extract it next to the other constants: `private const string BackdatedRefusalMessage = "official numbering refused: date is earlier than the last issued number";` and throw `new InvalidOperationException(BackdatedRefusalMessage)` at both sites.

ITEM 4 — INTERLEAVING VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY, NOT TAKEN ON TRUST. I traced the new test step by step and then confirmed the one assumption it silently depends on. Sequence inside the test: B's MaxAsync runs; the DbCommandInterceptor fires in ReaderExecutedAsync and lands LastSeq=2/LastDate=laterDate via ExecuteUpdateAsync (which deliberately bypasses the change tracker); MaxAsync nevertheless returns seedDate, so the pre-loop guard does NOT fire; the loop's FirstOrDefaultAsync returns the already-tracked stale instance (EF never overwrites a tracked entity's values on a tracking query), so attempt 1 sees LastDate=seedDate, passes the new check, increments 1->2 and issues an UPDATE whose concurrency token last_seq=1 no longer matches -> 0 rows -> DbUpdateConcurrencyException; ReloadAsync refreshes the row to LastSeq=2/laterDate; attempt 2 hits the new check and refuses. The load-bearing assumption is that the interceptor's UPDATE lands after the MAX aggregate is already computed. I proved that outside the repo with a standalone Microsoft.Data.Sqlite 10.0.12 console probe (scratchpad): an UPDATE executed on the same connection after ExecuteReader but before Read() leaves the reader returning the OLD max ("MAX seen by the already-executed reader: 2026-09-10 / MAX now: 2026-09-11"), because ExecuteReader steps the statement. So the refusal the test asserts genuinely comes from the new in-loop guard on the post-reload attempt, which matches the builder's own revert-and-rerun mutation check ("No exception was thrown" without the fix). Finding 1 above asks only that the test assert this itself rather than rely on that ordering.

ITEM 3 — SECURITY. After the fix there is no path on which a lost race lets an earlier-dated number commit: every retry iteration re-derives `row` and re-evaluates the watermark against that row's own freshly reloaded LastDate before LastSeq is touched, and a refusal throws before any mutation of the current iteration, so the caller's transaction rolls back with nothing written (the test's tail assertions confirm the persisted row stays at LastSeq 1 / seedDate). Uniqueness is unaffected: the composite PK (Kind, Year) still blocks a duplicate first insert and LastSeq.IsConcurrencyToken still blocks a stale increment, and the retry is still bounded at 5 with exhaustion surfacing as OfficialNumberConcurrencyException carrying the original DbUpdateException. No new false refusal is introduced — same-date issuance still passes (`today < row.LastDate.Date` is false on equality), a newly Added row has LastDate=today, and the 900/999 tests plus the two existing race tests still pass unchanged. One residual gap, inherent to the design and NOT introduced here, so not filed as a finding: a competing context that advances a DIFFERENT (kind, year) row to a later date does not collide with this row, so no retry occurs and only the TOCTOU-prone pre-loop MaxAsync guards that case (e.g. B issuing 2026-12-31 while A issues 2027-01-02). It is unreachable in practice on this database — SQLite serialises write transactions, and the test file documents empirically that a second connection cannot even open an overlapping transaction here — and closing it properly would need serialisation beyond this package's scope. Worth one line in B3's notes when the first real caller appears.
